Estimate the Hyperparameters by a Marginal Likelihood

Source: R/outer.R
reml.Rd

Build the criterion object that statmod() uses to choose a model's smooth hyperparameters by a marginal likelihood: the coefficients are integrated out by a Laplace approximation at the penalized mode, and the remainder is maximized in the hyperparameters. Pass the result as outer_criterion.

reml() integrates every coefficient that marginal does not name. ml() integrates only the penalized directions and profiles the rest. reml() is the default of statmod().

Usage

reml(information = observed_info(), marginal = NULL)

ml(information = observed_info(), marginal = NULL)

Arguments

information

The information that enters the determinant, an object that inherits from distributions7::Information:

  • distributions7::observed_info() (the default): the curvature of the log-likelihood at the data, which makes the criterion the Laplace approximation;

  • distributions7::expected_info(): the Fisher information, a function of the parameters alone. Its method selects how the expectation is obtained: NULL (the closed form of the family where it has one, and distributions7::expect_opg() otherwise), distributions7::expect_opg(), distributions7::expect_integrate() or distributions7::expect_mc() (see distributions7::expected_derivative_methods);

  • auto_info(): settled against the family by statmod() through outer_resolve(), as the expected information for a Student t, a skew t or a Cauchy response, whose observed information is not positive definite at an outlier, and as the observed information otherwise.

The expected information is used where the caller names it, as for a Student t whose degrees of freedom are modeled. The fitted model records the information used.

On the expected information, the method object defines the matrix and every derivative of it that the exact outer gradient and Hessian read, so that the derivatives are those of the criterion that is evaluated. With the closed form of the family, the derivative is the closed form of the derivative (every shipped family; the Hessian also needs the second derivative of the information, which every shipped family supplies except distributions7::enet_distrib()). With distributions7::expect_integrate() or distributions7::expect_mc(), it is the derivative of the expectation, which moves the density as well as the integrand. With distributions7::expect_opg(), the matrix is the outer product of the scores at the data and the derivative is its exact derivative at fixed data. A family without a closed form reads distributions7::expect_opg() for the matrix and for the derivatives when method is NULL. The outer product depends on the response, so the criterion built on it has exact derivatives and is not the Laplace approximation of an expectation. With method = NULL on a family without a closed form, the matrix of the criterion is therefore an estimate of the expected information, noisier than a computed expectation and about 25 times cheaper: on a density-only family (n = 300, ten basis functions) a fit took 0.8 s against 25.3 s for method = expect_integrate(identity = "score"), with smoothing parameters 12.57 and 13.00, against 13.02 for the observed information. The computed expectation is selected with method = expect_integrate(identity = "score"). distributions7::expect_mc() draws a new sample at each call of the matrix and of each derivative, so that its derivative is that of the expectation and not of the sampled matrix, and the outer search is noisy at the level of the Monte Carlo error. information_objects compares the three objects.

For a model with a structural term (modelterms7::gas(), modelterms7::regime(), a marginal break-point term) the criterion reads the observed information over the coefficients and the term's own parameters: auto_info() is settled as distributions7::observed_info(), and distributions7::expected_info() is an error.

marginal

Which distribution parameters have their unpenalized coefficients estimated by maximizing this criterion, instead of being read at the joint mode (ml()) or integrated (reml()). NULL, the default, names every parameter except the position, which is the family's first parameter. "none" names no parameter, "all" names every one, and a character vector names the parameters listed. With "all", reml() and ml() are the same criterion. For a multivariate family the default names no parameter, and naming one explicitly is an error. Where the model carries a penalty with a kink (a lasso, an elastic net, a SCAD or an MCP, in any equation), NULL names no parameter: the path that chooses the kinked penalty scores the model at the joint mode, and the fit returned is the model that it scored. A parameter named explicitly is still estimated on the criterion, at the value that the path chose. Where the family lacks the two derivatives that the criterion reads in some parameter (a Laplace response) and the model carries no smooth hyperparameter, the default criterion is not run at all, and a reml() or ml() passed by name is rejected.

Value

An OuterMethod() object of kind "reml" or "ml", whose hessian holds the object given as information and whose marginal is as supplied; its path settings are unused.

The criterion

At the penalized mode \(\hat\beta(\theta)\), $$\log L(\theta) = \ell(\hat\beta) - \rho(\hat\beta;\theta) + \frac{q}{2}\log 2\pi - \frac12\log|A'(H+S)A|,$$ with \(H\) the information of the log-likelihood, \(S\) the penalty's second derivative in the coefficients, and \(A\) an orthonormal basis of the subspace integrated over. The term \(\rho\) needs no correction: a penalties7 penalty keeps its normalizing constant, so it is exactly minus a log prior density, and for a quadratic penalty that constant carries the \(-\frac{r}{2}\log\lambda\) and the log pseudo-determinant that a marginal criterion needs. Written out, the expression reproduces Wood's (2011) REML criterion term for term.

The effective degrees of freedom of the fit

The effective degrees of freedom stored in the fitted model (fit@edf), the share of each term in \(\mathrm{tr}[(H+S)^{-1}H]\), are read on the information of the criterion: distributions7::observed_info() by default, or the distributions7::expected_info() object with its method. The count is not part of the criterion here, but the standard errors of the same fit read the same default matrix, so the count and the standard errors of a summary agree. summary.StatmodFit() recomputes the count when its vcov_type names the other matrix. For a positive semidefinite \(H\) the total lies in \([0, p]\), with \(p\) the number of coefficients; an indefinite observed information can give a direction of negative curvature a negative share, and the summary then adds a note.

What each one integrates

Write \(\gamma\) for the unpenalized coefficients of the parameters that marginal names, and \(u\) for every other coefficient. The criterion is maximized in \(\gamma\) together with the hyperparameters. At each value of \(\gamma\), the coefficients \(u\) are set to the penalized mode.

reml() integrates every coefficient in \(u\). An unpenalized one is integrated under a flat prior; the absence of a penalty amounts to a flat prior. ml() integrates only the directions in the range space of the penalty, so an unpenalized coefficient in \(u\) is read at the mode. An ordinary covariate is unpenalized. The linear component of a Demmler-Reinsch smooth is unpenalized too, because the penalty of that smooth does not act on it.

With marginal = "all", \(\gamma\) holds every unpenalized coefficient. The two criteria then integrate the same directions, and they are the same function.

Where the criterion estimates coefficients, a coefficient that the model does not identify at the first fit is left out of the determinant for the whole search and stays free in the inner fit. This corresponds to the REML log-likelihood of stats::lm() (logLik(fit, REML = TRUE)), which uses the rank of the design in place of its number of columns.

Where a dispersion and a shape are estimated

By default marginal names every parameter except the position, which is the family's first parameter: the location, or the scale for a family with no location, such as distributions7::weibull1_distrib(). For a gaussian mixed model this is the REML of lme and glmmTMB. The coefficients of the mean are integrated, and \(\sigma\) is maximized on the criterion. Without any penalty, reml() returns the \(\sigma\) of stats::lm(), \(\sqrt{\mathrm{rss}/(n-p)}\), and its criterion equals logLik(lm(...), REML = TRUE). ml() returns \(\sqrt{\mathrm{rss}/n}\). If agec is defined as age - 11, the model distance ~ agec + random(~ agec | Subject) on nlme::Orthodont gives the estimates and the criterion of lme.

marginal = "none" gives the convention of gamlss and of mgcv's gaulss: every parameter of the distribution is read at the joint mode of the penalized likelihood. That estimate ignores the degrees of freedom of the coefficients estimated beside it, so a dispersion read there is biased downwards. Where a dispersion carries a random effect of its own, the bias at the joint mode is larger than the bias on the criterion.

Where some coefficients of the location are integrated, the estimate depends on the parametrization of the family. The dispersion of distributions7::gamma1_distrib() and the variance of distributions7::gamma2_distrib(), \(\sigma^2 = \phi\mu^2\), differ under reml(), because the second contains the integrated mean. With "all" the criterion does not depend on the parametrization.

Some configurations are not covered, and marginal_coords() lists them: a structural term anywhere in the model, a block that is a working linearization (a sharp modelterms7::jump() or modelterms7::jseg()) anywhere in the model, a block that moves with its coefficients in the parameter's own equation, and a quadratic penalty in that equation whose null space is not spanned by coordinates. In each case a parameter that the default names keeps the convention of "none", and a parameter named explicitly is rejected. Beside a penalty with a kink the default names no parameter, and a parameter named explicitly is estimated on the criterion, and the coordinates that the kinked penalty covers are excluded. For a multivariate family the default names no parameter, and an explicit marginal other than "none" is an error.

Which hyperparameters

The criterion estimates the hyperparameters of the terms fitted in one system, meaning the terms whose penalty is twice differentiable. A lasso, a SCAD or an MCP has a kink, its coefficients are estimated by a method of their own, and a Laplace approximation is undefined at a point where the second derivative does not exist. Those hyperparameters are not on the outer search. statmod() chooses them by a path under sparse_criterion, which is bic() by default and can also be aic() or cv().

The exact gradient

The criterion has an exact gradient on the observed and on the expected information, for every penalty whose derivatives in the coefficients and the hyperparameters are available, as those of modelterms7::s(), modelterms7::te() and any penalties7::quadratic_penalty() are; a model with a modelterms7::regime() term has none. The gradient, and the Hessian where it is exact, are supplied to the search. The default optimizer is optimizers7::newton() with a bounded step where the Hessian is exact and steers the search, optimizers7::lbfgs() where only the gradient is exact, optimizers7::brent() for a single coordinate without a gradient, and optimizers7::nelder_mead() otherwise. A simplex needs one vertex per dimension and a quasi-Newton method does not, so an exact gradient saves criterion evaluations once there are two or more hyperparameters.

ML needs a null basis

ml() reads the null space of every penalty over which it integrates, because the null space determines which directions are profiled. penalties7::is_proper() identifies a penalty with no null space, and penalties7::penalty_null_basis() returns the null space of a quadratic, structured, additive or separable penalty. A penalty that provides neither is rejected by name, and the criterion does not assume a subspace for it.

References

Wood, S. N. (2011). Fast stable restricted maximum likelihood and marginal likelihood estimation of semiparametric generalized linear models. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 73(1), 3–36.

See also

aic(), bic() and cv() for the prediction-error criteria, information_objects for the argument information, statmod() for where these are passed, hyper() for reading back what they chose.

Examples

set.seed(1)
dd <- data.frame(x = runif(200, -2, 2))
dd$y <- sin(1.4 * dd$x) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)

fit <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)), distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd,
               outer_criterion = reml())

# The smoothing parameter was estimated, and hyper() reports it.
hyper(fit)
#>   parameter                         term   name estimate  held source   id
#> 1        mu s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)) lambda  3.21673 FALSE   reml <NA>

# ML profiles the unpenalized directions instead of integrating them, so
# it shrinks a little less. The gap is small here because only two of the
# ten coefficients are unpenalized; it widens with the fixed effects.
fml <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)), distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd,
               outer_criterion = ml())
c(reml = hyper(fit)$estimate, ml = hyper(fml)$estimate)
#>     reml       ml 
#> 3.216730 3.205381 
c(reml = sum(fit@edf$edf), ml = sum(fml@edf$edf))
#>     reml       ml 
#> 8.555773 8.567577 

# The marginal log-likelihood, which these criteria maximize, is only
# available where one of them ran.
logLik(fit, loglik_type = "marginal")
#> 'log Lik.' -53.66395 (df=4)
